title: The 2026-27 Budget: Update on Local Control Funding Formula Costs
key_claim: California credits districts with the higher of current-year, prior-year or three-year-average attendance; in 2025-26, 38% of districts were funded on the rolling average and the device credited districts with roughly 74,000 more ADA, 1.5% above a current-year count, while statewide enrolment fell 1.2% in one year and 7.8% since 2016-17.
frame_summary: This source argues that California's attendance-averaging rules are a measurable and costed cushion that keeps district funding above what current enrolment would generate.
verbatim_quote: For funding purposes, the state credits school districts with their ADA in the current year, prior year, or the average of three prior years, whichever is higher.
verbatim_list: The ability to use attendance from the prior year or the average of the three prior years results in districts being credited with roughly 74,000 more ADA (1.5 percent) than if the state funded districts on current year ADA only.

The preliminary data for 2025-26 shows 43 percent of school districts are expected to be funded on their current year ADA, 19 percent on their prior year ADA, and 38 percent on the rolling average of their three prior years of ADA.
Census Day enrollment in 2025-26 has declined 1.2 percent (about 72,000 students) from 2024-25.
overall enrollment for school districts and charter schools has declined 7.8 percent (close to 485,000 students) since 2016-17
Compared to 2024-25, more districts are expected to be funded on their current year ADA (up from 33 percent).

title: Declining Enrollment in America's Public Schools: How States Can Respond Strategically
date_evidence: Policy Brief by Carrie Hahnel (Bellwether) and Jason Willis (WestEd) June 2026 (c) 2026 Bellwether and WestEd
key_claim: 40 states and DC are projected to lose public school enrolment through 2030-31, costing an estimated $11.5 billion a year in state revenues; 68% of districts lost enrolment between 2018-19 and 2023-24 while most still operate roughly the same number of schools, a mismatch federal COVID relief temporarily masked.
frame_summary: This source argues that states, not districts, must redesign funding and planning systems because the tools used in past revenue shocks cannot absorb a permanent demographic contraction.
verbatim_quote: Bellwether has found that 68 percent of K–12 districts experienced enrollment declines between 2018–19 and 2023–24. However, most of these districts still operate roughly the same number of schools
verbatim_list: the nation's public education system could lose $11.5 billion in state revenues annually by 2030–31
a mismatch that federal COVID-19 funding relief temporarily masked
Some states have hold-harmless provisions or legacy allocation structures that preserve past funding levels for districts without a set end date, even as enrollment declines.
A more sustainable and responsive approach is to use dynamic hold-harmless policies or tapering mechanisms that allow funding to gradually adjust as enrollment shrinks.
notes: The PDF title page carries the month only (June 2026). 30 June 2026 is used as the publication date because K-12 Dive reported the brief as newly released on that date. Disclosed in the delivery message.

title: The Hidden Geography of School Enrollment Decline: Exurban Districts Are Booming While Others Shrink
key_claim: Enrolment decline is geographically uneven: fringe (exurban) public schools gained 6% or 380,000 students over the decade while city schools lost 6% or 950,000, so growth and contraction now sit inside the same metropolitan area.
frame_summary: This source argues that a national enrolment decline conceals a redistribution of students toward exurban districts, so policy aimed at the national average will misfit most individual districts.
verbatim_quote: Enrollment in fringe public schools grew by a remarkable 6% (380,000 students) over the last decade
verbatim_list: Between 2015 and 2024, enrollment in fringe public schools in the San Antonio-New Braunfels metropolitan area rose by 40%, while enrollment in San Antonio city schools decreased by 7%.
In fall 2024, 6.4 million students attended a public school in a fringe region of the country

title: NYC's $1.9 billion dilemma: How long can schools be 'held harmless' for enrollment losses?

title: Fewer students, too many schools: Communities face closures, consolidations
key_claim: More than 1,000 public schools closed nationwide in 2025-26, the fourth consecutive annual rise; US enrolment fell from 50.8 million to 49.4 million between 2019 and 2024 and is projected to reach about 46.9 million by 2031, with states including Vermont and Illinois legislating to encourage rather than compel mergers.
frame_summary: This source argues that school closure has become a national rather than local phenomenon and that states are now actively steering consolidation while stopping short of mandating it.
verbatim_quote: Just because your number of students goes down, doesn't mean that your fixed costs go down
verbatim_list: More than 1,000 public schools closed nationwide in the 2025-26 school year, according to preliminary National Center for Education Statistics data. It's the fourth year in a row that school closures have gone up.
Nationwide, U.S. enrollment dropped from nearly 50.8 million to almost 49.4 million K-12 students between 2019 and 2024, or 2.8%, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.
That number is projected to drop even further to about 46.9 million students by 2031, the center data estimated.
Beginning this year, the state can provide up to $16,000 for studies examining enrollment projections, school capacity, potential building closures, transportation, finances and academic programs.
Vermont has lost about 20% of its student enrollment over the past two decades

title: School districts assigned to new merger discussion groups
key_claim: Vermont has grouped its 119 school districts into 18 merger study committees that must hold first meetings by 15 October 2026, report to the state by February and September 2027 and put mergers to local votes on Town Meeting Day 2028, with core terms of Act 170 such as good-faith participation still undefined.
frame_summary: This source argues that Vermont's merger process is running to a statutory timetable that is ahead of the guidance districts need to comply with it.
verbatim_quote: The change in assignments comes just weeks before committees are expected to hold their first meetings, which must occur by Oct. 15.
verbatim_list: The new assignments announced Friday group the state's 119 districts into 18 committees.
Under Act 170, school districts will vote on mergers on Town Meeting Day in 2028.
Then each study committee has to submit a final report to the state in September 2027 detailing which of its members — if any — are merging.
The law says that districts in a committee should collectively enroll at least 2,000 students
The regional facilitators, who will help districts make the best decisions they can with informed data, are paid $150 an hour, with a $50,000 limit for the entire committee process
Facilitators must submit a report to the state on Feb. 1 with an update on committee work
he's in the process of refining a standard for what “good faith” participation means

title: Enrollment Down, Funding Up
key_claim: Reporting peer-reviewed work by Matthew Lee and Benjamin Scafidi in Education Finance and Policy covering 1998 to 2019, EdChoice argues that districts losing enrolment saw larger increases in per-pupil expenditure than growing districts, because revenue fell by less than enrolment, and that they spent the difference on more staff rather than higher pay.
frame_summary: This source argues that the belief that falling enrolment cuts district funding is a myth, and that hold-harmless devices have historically left shrinking districts better resourced per pupil than growing ones.
verbatim_quote: districts with declining enrollment experienced significantly larger increases in total and current expenditures per pupil relative to districts with growing enrollment
verbatim_list: These advantages with respect to expenditures and resources were possible because declining districts saw state and especially local and federal revenue declines that were smaller, in absolute value, than their declines in enrollment—or they experienced increases in revenues as enrollment declined.
This pattern translated into much larger increases in total staffing and teachers per 100 students in declining districts relative to growing districts.
They look at enrollment changes and expenditures from 1998 to 2019.
notes: Tier 4 advocacy source used only for the counter-argument, where its position is the strongest available objection. The underlying study is peer-reviewed; EdChoice is the accessible verified record of it and its own framing is disclosed as advocacy.
